# LiteLLM #34399: multi-deployment retries ignore Retry-After

- Status at capture: open
- Upstream: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34399
- Pinned source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

`Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry` honors an upstream `Retry-After` header
for a single deployment but returns zero immediately when another healthy
deployment exists. That assumes deployments have independent limits. In
practice, several deployments can share one upstream quota, so instant retries
hammer the throttled service and exhaust the retry budget before its backoff
window ends.

Acceptance criteria:

1. A focused test represents two deployments sharing a rate-limited upstream.
2. An explicit upstream backoff is not silently discarded merely because a
   sibling deployment is healthy.
3. Immediate failover remains possible when no upstream backoff applies.
4. The change states the precedence between provider backoff and router retry
   policy.

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_31be9c3c708a4a5797d50a579c137587",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/github/redwood/pr-19820-api-gateway-fallback-timeout-tuning.json",
    "title": "API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/github",
    "content": "{\n  \"repo\": \"redwood\",\n  \"pr_number\": \"19820\",\n  \"title\": \"API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses\",\n  \"author\": \"Peter Holtz\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-11\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-01-13\",\n  \"merged_at\": \"2026-01-13\",\n  \"state\": \"merged\",\n  \"base_branch\": \"main\",\n  \"head_branch\": \"feature/failover-gateway-timeout-retryafter\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Miles Thornton\",\n    \"Mina Haddad\",\n    \"Ravi Menon\",\n    \"Allison Grant\",\n    \"Tom\\u00e1\\u0161 Nov\\u00e1k\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"sre\",\n    \"routing\",\n    \"gateway\",\n    \"reliability\",\n    \"failover\",\n    \"observability\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_linear\": [\n    \"ENG-2419\",\n    \"ENG-2411\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_jira\": [\n    \"SUP-25310\",\n    \"SUP-25322\"\n  ],\n  \"ci_status\": \"pass\",\n  \"files_changed_count\": \"19\",\n  \"additions\": \"463\",\n  \"deletions\": \"211\",\n  \"breaking_change\": \"false\",\n  \"release_notes\": \"- During regional impairments/failover, the gateway enforces a smaller retry budget and tighter per-hop timeouts to reduce thundering herd.\\n- Standardizes explicit overload responses with Retry-After for upstream exhaustion (helps clients back off cleanly).\\n- Adds metrics for overload responses + retry budget exhaustion to support failover dashboards.\",\n  \"content\": \"Title: API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses\\n\\nContext\\nDuring failover drills and a couple of real partial impairments, we saw gateway retries + long tail timeouts amplify load. When a region is impaired (or when routing is actively moving traffic), the existing retry budgets can cause: (1) request fan-out across regions (client retries + gateway retries), (2) work amplification against already-constrained capacity, (3) noisy error/latency signals that delay decisive failover.\\n\\nThis PR tightens timeouts/retry behavior when failover is active or when the upstream is overloaded, and introduces explicit Retry-After responses for overload so clients can apply deterministic backoff.\\n\\nWhat changed (high level)\\n- Retry budget policy:\\n  - Introduce a \\u201cfailover mode\\u201d retry budget profile that is automatically enabled when routing marks a route/region as degraded OR when the gateway observes consecutive upstream overload signals.\\n  - In failover mode we reduce max retries and cap total retry time (wall clock) per request.\\n- Timeout tuning:\\n  - Reduce upstream connect + response header timeouts in failover mode (we prefer fast failure + reroute over slow hangs).\\n  - Ensure streaming requests fail quickly on cross-region redirect paths so the client can reconnect (ties to ENG-2422 follow-up).\\n- Explicit overload response:\\n  - When upstream returns/indicates overload (or circuit breaker opens), gateway responds with 429 (or 503 where semantically required) and sets Retry-After with a bounded jittered value.\\n  - Adds an internal header to preserve reason codes for debugging while avoiding leaking internal topology.\\n- Circuit breaker integration:\\n  - Treat circuit-breaker open as authoritative overload for retry policy evaluation.\\n  - Do not retry non-idempotent requests unless the request is explicitly marked idempotent by the client (existing behavior preserved; now stricter under failover mode).\\n\\nBehavior details\\n- Overload response mapping:\\n  - If upstream is saturated or CB is open: respond 429 Too Many Requests (Hosted API) with `Retry-After: <seconds>`.\\n  - If endpoint requires 503 by contract (some internal control-plane paths): respond 503 Service Unavailable with `Retry-After`.\\n  - Streaming: if redirect/failover triggers mid-stream, return a terminal frame that includes an error code and Retry-After guidance; clients should reconnect (see notes below).\\n\\n- Retry budget:\\n  - Normal mode defaults unchanged.\\n  - Failover mode:\\n    - max_attempts: 2 (1 initial + 1 retry)\\n    - max_total_retry_time: 800ms (non-streaming) / 1200ms (streaming handshake)\\n    - backoff: exponential with decorrelated jitter, capped at 250ms\\n\\nWhy this is safe\\n- Changes are gated behind a feature flag: `gateway.failover_tuned_retry_budget` (default OFF in prod; ON in staging).\\n- Retry-After is only emitted for overload/circuit-breaker conditions (not for generic 5xx).\\n- We preserve idempotency rules and further restrict retries under failover mode.\\n\\nObservability\\nNew metrics (names are illustrative; see files below for exact names):\\n- `gateway_overload_responses_total{route,tier,reason}`\\n- `gateway_retry_budget_exhausted_total{route,tier,mode}`\\n- `gateway_upstream_timeout_total{route,tier,mode}`\\nAlso adds log annotations when failover mode is entered/exited for a route.\\n\\nFiles / areas changed\\n- api-gateway\\n  - retry_budget.go: add failover profile + gating logic\\n  - timeouts.go: per-mode upstream timeouts + defaults\\n  - overload_response.go: 429/503 mapping + Retry-After\\n  - streaming/termination.go: terminal frame mapping for overload\\n- config\\n  - gateway feature flag config + safe defaults\\n- docs (internal)\\n  - runbook snippet: how to recognize Retry-After overload vs regional impairment\\n\\nIllustrative snippet\\n- Example overload response headers:\\n  - `HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests`\\n  - `Retry-After: 2`\\n  - `x-redwood-overload: 1` (internal-only in logs; not forwarded to clients)\\n\\nTesting\\n- Unit tests:\\n  - retry budget switches to failover mode when routing marks region degraded\\n  - retry budget switches to failover mode when CB open trips\\n  - Retry-After header present and within bounds (1\\u20135s with jitter)\\n  - Non-idempotent requests not retried under failover mode\\n- Integration tests (staging):\\n  - Simulated overload returns 429 + Retry-After and reduces repeat request rate\\n  - Cross-region redirect path does not exceed max_total_retry_time\\n\\nRollout plan\\n1) Enable in staging for all tenants + validate metrics / no regression (24h).\\n2) Enable in prod for canary routes only (Hosted: /v1/chat, /v1/completions; Dedicated: selected pools).\\n3) Expand to all routes once burn-rate alerts show reduced oscillation and we confirm no client compatibility issues.\\n\\nNotes / follow-ups\\n- Client-facing guidance will be updated in the SDK docs to respect Retry-After (tracked separately; see redwood-docs PR).\\n- Streaming reconnect improvements are in progress (ENG-2422 / PR-19821).\\n\\nChecklist\\n- [x] Feature-flagged and default OFF in prod\\n- [x] Unit tests added\\n- [x] Added metrics + dashboard hooks\\n- [x] Verified no PII in overload reason logs\\n- [x] SRE sign-off for game day readiness\\n\\nCommits\\n1) gateway: add failover-mode retry budget profile\\n2) gateway: tune upstream timeouts for failover mode\\n3) gateway: implement overload responses with Retry-After\\n4) gateway: add metrics + log annotations\\n5) tests: cover retry/timeout/overload behavior\\n\\nReview conversation (highlights)\\n- Miles Thornton: \\u201cWe need to be very explicit about when failover mode activates. Please ensure it\\u2019s not driven by a single noisy 5xx signal.\\u201d\\n  - Peter Holtz (author): \\u201cAgreed. Activation is based on routing \\u2018degraded\\u2019 OR circuit-breaker open OR sustained overload counter for N=20 requests in 30s; not generic 5xx burn. Added test + docs in code comments.\\u201d\\n\\n- Mina Haddad: \\u201cCan we guarantee we don\\u2019t flip-flop between normal/failover budgets?\\u201d\\n  - Peter: \\u201cAdded hold-down timer of 2 minutes after entering failover mode; exit requires 5 minutes healthy + CB closed. (Matches general anti-flap guidance; aligns with ongoing ADR work.)\\u201d\\n\\n- Allison Grant: \\u201cMetric label cardinality: please don\\u2019t include tenant_id or model in the new overload metrics.\\u201d\\n  - Peter: \\u201cConfirmed: route + tier + coarse reason only.       "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/github\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/github/redwood/pr-19820-api-gateway-fallback-timeout-tuning.json\nConnector: github\nWorkspace: redwood\n\nwhat changed ( high level ) - retry budget policy : - introduce a “ failover mode ” retry budget profile that is automatically enabled when routing marks a route / region as degraded or when the gateway observes consecutive upstream overload signals. - in failover mode we reduce max retries and cap total retry time ( wall clock ) per request. - timeout tuning : - reduce upstream connect + response header timeouts in failover mode ( we prefer fast failure + reroute over slow hangs ). - ensure streaming requests fail quickly on cross - region redirect paths so the client can reconnect ( ties to eng - 2422 follow - up ). - explicit overload response : - when upstream returns / indicates overload ( or circuit breaker opens ), gateway",

{
  "repo": "redwood",
  "pr_number": "19820",
  "title": "API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses",
  "author": "Peter Holtz",
  "created_at": "2026-01-11",
  "updated_at": "2026-01-13",
  "merged_at": "2026-01-13",
  "state": "merged",
  "base_branch": "main",
  "head_branch": "feature/failover-gateway-timeout-retryafter",
  "reviewers": [
    "Miles Thornton",
    "Mina Haddad",
    "Ravi Menon",
    "Allison Grant",
    "Tomáš Novák"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "sre",
    "routing",
    "gateway",
    "reliability",
    "failover",
    "observability"
  ],
  "linked_linear": [
    "ENG-2419",
    "ENG-2411"
  ],
  "linked_jira": [
    "SUP-25310",
    "SUP-25322"
  ],
  "ci_status": "pass",
  "files_changed_count": "19",
  "additions": "463",
  "deletions": "211",
  "breaking_change": "false",
  "release_notes": "- During regional impairments/failover, the gateway enforces a smaller retry budget and tighter per-hop timeouts to reduce thundering herd.
- Standardizes explicit overload responses with Retry-After for upstream exhaustion (helps clients back off cleanly).
- Adds metrics for overload responses + retry budget exhaustion to support failover dashboards.",
  "content": "Title: API gateway: tune fallback timeouts + retry budgets during regional failover; add Retry-After overload responses

Context
During failover drills and a couple of real partial impairments, we saw gateway retries + long tail timeouts amplify load. When a region is impaired (or when routing is actively moving traffic), the existing retry budgets can cause: (1) request fan-out across regions (client retries + gateway retries), (2) work amplification against already-constrained capacity, (3) noisy error/latency signals that delay decisive failover.

This PR tightens timeouts/retry behavior when failover is active or when the upstream is overloaded, and introduces explicit Retry-After responses for overload so clients can apply deterministic backoff.

What changed (high level)
- Retry budget policy:
  - Introduce a “failover mode” retry budget profile that is automatically enabled when routing marks a route/region as degraded OR when the gateway observes consecutive upstream overload signals.
  - In failover mode we reduce max retries and cap total retry time (wall clock) per request.
- Timeout tuning:
  - Reduce upstream connect + response header timeouts in failover mode (we prefer fast failure + reroute over slow hangs).
  - Ensure streaming requests fail quickly on cross-region redirect paths so the client can reconnect (ties to ENG-2422 follow-up).
- Explicit overload response:
  - When upstream returns/indicates overload (or circuit breaker opens), gateway responds with 429 (or 503 where semantically required) and sets Retry-After with a bounded jittered value.
  - Adds an internal header to preserve reason codes for debugging while avoiding leaking internal topology.
- Circuit breaker integration:
  - Treat circuit-breaker open as authoritative overload for retry policy evaluation.
  - Do not retry non-idempotent requests unless the request is explicitly marked idempotent by the client (existing behavior preserved; now stricter under failover mode).

Behavior details
- Overload response mapping:
  - If upstream is saturated or CB is open: respond 429 Too Many Requests (Hosted API) with `Retry-After: <seconds>`.
  - If endpoint requires 503 by contract (some internal control-plane paths): respond 503 Service Unavailable with `Retry-After`.
  - Streaming: if redirect/failover triggers mid-stream, return a terminal frame that includes an error code and Retry-After guidance; clients should reconnect (see notes below).

- Retry budget:
  - Normal mode defaults unchanged.
  - Failover mode:
    - max_attempts: 2 (1 initial + 1 retry)
    - max_total_retry_time: 800ms (non-streaming) / 1200ms (streaming handshake)
    - backoff: exponential with decorrelated jitter, capped at 250ms

Why this is safe
- Changes are gated behind a feature flag: `gateway.failover_tuned_retry_budget` (default OFF in prod; ON in staging).
- Retry-After is only emitted for overload/circuit-breaker conditions (not for generic 5xx).
- We preserve idempotency rules and further restrict retries under failover mode.

Observability
New metrics (names are illustrative; see files below for exact names):
- `gateway_overload_responses_total{route,tier,reason}`
- `gateway_retry_budget_exhausted_total{route,tier,mode}`
- `gateway_upstream_timeout_total{route,tier,mode}`
Also adds log annotations when failover mode is entered/exited for a route.

Files / areas changed
- api-gateway
  - retry_budget.go: add failover profile + gating logic
  - timeouts.go: per-mode upstream timeouts + defaults
  - overload_response.go: 429/503 mapping + Retry-After
  - streaming/termination.go: terminal frame mapping for overload
- config
  - gateway feature flag config + safe defaults
- docs (internal)
  - runbook snippet: how to recognize Retry-After overload vs regional impairment

Illustrative snippet
- Example overload response headers:
  - `HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests`
  - `Retry-After: 2`
  - `x-redwood-overload: 1` (internal-only in logs; not forwarded to clients)

Testing
- Unit tests:
  - retry budget switches to failover mode when routing marks region degraded
  - retry budget switches to failover mode when CB open trips
  - Retry-After header present and within bounds (1–5s with jitter)
  - Non-idempotent requests not retried under failover mode
- Integration tests (staging):
  - Simulated overload returns 429 + Retry-After and reduces repeat request rate
  - Cross-region redirect path does not exceed max_total_retry_time

Rollout plan
1) Enable in staging for all tenants + validate metrics / no regression (24h).
2) Enable in prod for canary routes only (Hosted: /v1/chat, /v1/completions; Dedicated: selected pools).
3) Expand to all routes once burn-rate alerts show reduced oscillation and we confirm no client compatibility issues.

Notes / follow-ups
- Client-facing guidance will be updated in the SDK docs to respect Retry-After (tracked separately; see redwood-docs PR).
- Streaming reconnect improvements are in progress (ENG-2422 / PR-19821).

Checklist
- [x] Feature-flagged and default OFF in prod
- [x] Unit tests added
- [x] Added metrics + dashboard hooks
- [x] Verified no PII in overload reason logs
- [x] SRE sign-off for game day readiness

Commits
1) gateway: add failover-mode retry budget profile
2) gateway: tune upstream timeouts for failover mode
3) gateway: implement overload responses with Retry-After
4) gateway: add metrics + log annotations
5) tests: cover retry/timeout/overload behavior

Review conversation (highlights)
- Miles Thornton: “We need to be very explicit about when failover mode activates. Please ensure it’s not driven by a single noisy 5xx signal.”
  - Peter Holtz (author): “Agreed. Activation is based on routing ‘degraded’ OR circuit-breaker open OR sustained overload counter for N=20 requests in 30s; not generic 5xx burn. Added test + docs in code comments.”

- Mina Haddad: “Can we guarantee we don’t flip-flop between normal/failover budgets?”
  - Peter: “Added hold-down timer of 2 minutes after entering failover mode; exit requires 5 minutes healthy + CB closed. (Matches general anti-flap guidance; aligns with ongoing ADR work.)”

- Allison Grant: “Metric label cardinality: please don’t include tenant_id or model in the new overload metrics.”
  - Peter: “Confirmed: route + tier + coarse reason only. No tenant/model labels. Added comment + lint check for disallowed labels.”

- Tomáš Novák: “Please add a runbook note so on-call knows Retry-After spikes are expected during protective shedding and not necessarily a routing bug.”
  - Peter: “Added internal runbook snippet + log annotation pointers.”

CI
- Build: pass
- Unit tests: pass
- Lint: pass
- One initial failure due to flaky integration test timing; reran after tightening deterministic clock in the test harness.

Merge outcome
Merged (squash) into main on 2026-01-13.

Related
- Linear: ENG-2419 (Update API gateway circuit breakers), ENG-2411 (Umbrella)
- Jira: SUP-25310 (Transient 5xx during planned routing test), SUP-25322 (Streaming disconnects during region redirect)
- Follow-ups: PR-19821 (streaming reconnect), PR-19827 (standardized overload responses + Retry-After in dataplane)",

  "content_field_names": [
    "content"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_31be9c3c708a4a5797d50a579c137587"

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/google_drive",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"SRE Incident Review: client-side retry storm & emergency quota policy change\",\n  \"owner\": \"Ayesha Patel\",\n  \"drive_area\": \"shared_drives\",\n  \"path\": \"shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/\",\n  \"doc_type\": \"doc\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-18\",\n  \"last_modified\": \"2025-11-25\",\n  \"collaborators\": [\n    \"Miguel Ramos\",\n    \"Jinsoo Park\",\n    \"Priya Desai\"\n  ],\n  \"team\": \"eng-sre\",\n  \"status\": \"in_review\",\n  \"tags\": [\n    \"incident-review\",\n    \"rate-limiting\",\n    \"quota\",\n    \"retry-storm\",\n    \"runbook-update\",\n    \"postmortem-like\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_artifacts\": [\n    \"JIRA: SRE-8472\",\n    \"Slack: #oncall-2025-11-18-thread\",\n    \"PR: github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4321\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"Summary:\\n- 2025-11-18 09:42 UTC: sudden surge of short-lived requests from a small set of client IPs and API keys triggered cascading retries and pushed backend queues into high tail-latency.\\n- Impact: transient 5xx spikes for hosted API customers (peak 12% increased error rate for 18 minutes), increased GPU queue latency, several canary routes failed, billing/usage accounting gaps in one shard.\\n- Immediate mitigation: emergency quota policy change (temporary per-key unified cap + soft-deny with Retry-After headers) and WAF rule to block obvious bot patterns.\\n\\nWhy this doc exists:\\n- capture timeline and decisions while fresh\\n- propose concrete runbook edits for emergency quota changes and retry guidance to clients\\n- outline monitoring/alerts to detect similar patterns earlier\\n\\nTimeline (rough):\\n- 09:40 UTC: first anomalous traffic flow observed by anomaly detector; alert went to #anomalies but not severe enough to page.\\n- 09:42 UTC: external customers report elevated 5xx; SLO alerts fire (latency p95 and error-rate).\\n- 09:44 UTC: on-call paged; initial investigation shows thousands of ~100ms requests concentrated in short bursts per API key.\\n- 09:46 UTC: SRE rotated through quick checks: token bucket levels (Redis ok), leaky queue lengths rising in Kube autoscale group.\\n- 09:50 UTC: discovered client-side library had new default retry policy that retries aggressively on 429/5xx; many clients updated in last 48h.\\n- 09:53 UTC: implemented emergency temporary per-key cap (global cap override) and returned 429 with Retry-After=10s to suspected keys.\\n- 10:00 UTC: WAF rule deployed to drop obvious bot UA patterns and high-rate IPs; errors fell back toward baseline by ~10:15.\\n- 10:20 UTC: rollback of temporary cap for keys with good signal; monitoring kept on.\\n\\nRoot cause analysis (hypothesis and evidence):\\n- Primary cause: client-side change (library v2.3.0) introduced more aggressive retry-on-429 behavior. Evidence: correlating release metadata from SDK with surge start; SDK release notes mention optimistic fast-retry.\\n- Amplifier: no circuit-breaker behavior in gateway for repeated bursts per key; rate-limiter default token-bucket config allowed short bursts beyond safe thresholds.\\n- Secondary: monitoring threshold design \\u2014 anomaly detector used 1m aggregation window; the traffic pattern had 10s micro-bursts. Alerting missed early micro-burst signal.\\n- WAF helped but was reactive; bot signatures were not matching some legitimate replaying clients.\\n\\nDetection and observability gaps:\\n- No short-window microburst alert. Need 10s and 30s windows for p95/reqs-per-key metrics.\\n- Per-key telemetry lacked recent histogram of retry counts; we didn't see rapid escalation of retries until SLOs tripped.\\n- Debug logs for gateway dropped requests were sampled too aggressively; by the time we tried to inspect, sample not representative.\\n\\nImmediate mitigations taken (what worked/why):\\n- Emergency per-key unified cap: stopped the worst offenders quickly. Worked because it prevented token bucket pumping across all shards.\\n- WAF rule: dropped clearly non-compliant UA/IP patterns, shaving off the noise.\\n- Sending 429 with Retry-After: encouraged well-behaved clients to backoff rather than flood retry loops.\\n\\nWhat didn't work / surprises:\\n- Autoscaling didn't buy us out \\u2014 short microbursts saturated queueing and raised tail latencies even though overall capacity nominal.\\n- Some internal debug tooling relied on per-minute aggregation and hid the pattern.\\n\\nRunbook (draft) \\u2014 emergency steps for future retry storms and quota emergencies:\\n1) Triage (first 5 minutes):\\n  - confirm SLO triggers (latency/error rate).\\n  - identify top 20 keys/IPs by request rate in last 60s (query metrics-raw).\\n  - check gateway token-bucket fill-rates and Redis latency.\\n2) Short-window mitigation (5-15 minutes):\\n  - apply temporary per-key cap: unify cap to 100 reqs/min per key (config path: /config/emergency/per_key_cap_override).\\n  - switch gateway behavior to soft-deny (429 + Retry-After 10s) instead of hard-block for suspected keys.\\n  - enable high-resolution tracing for affected shards (10s sampling) and increase debug log retention for next 1h.\\n3) Blocking (if ongoing >15 mins):\\n  - apply WAF rule to block IP ranges with >X reqs/10s and UA regex match. Document rule ID and reason.\\n  - deploy temporary global backpressure: degrade non-essential routes (embeddings low-priority batch routes) to preserve core generation throughput.\\n4) Communication & customer handling:\\n  - notify CS and post in #service-incidents with incident summary + affected keys list (redact PII).\\n  - for keys likely owned by customers, coordinate with CS to email recommended client SDK updates and guidance on backoff.\\n5) Recovery & rollback:\\n  - progressively relax per-key cap for keys showing good behavior for 30m.\\n  - remove WAF rule once traffic stabilizes for 60m and no reappearance.\\n\\nRunbook edits to make (todo list):\\n- Add a short-window microburst alert (10s/30s windows) for per-key QPS and retry-counts.\\n- Add a checklist for creating safe WAF rules: pre-approved rule templates + emergency rule naming convention.\\n- Document default gateway retry/circuit-breaker config and add a safe conservative profile for hosted tier.\\n- Add SDK coordination play: preflight check in release PRs to flag retry policy changes and notify SRE when aggressive defaults are introduced.\\n\\nMonitoring / dashboards to add or adjust:\\n- per-key 10s QPS heatmap (top 200 keys), highlight spikes in last 30m\\n- retry-counts histogram per key (30s buckets) and moving average\\n- queue length percentile (p95/p99) with 10s resolution for GPU workers\\n- dashboard tile for active emergency caps and WAF rules (who/why applied)\\n\\nCustomer & partner follow-up (notes to CS/Product):\\n- Recommend customers pin SDK to v2.2.x while they validate v2.3.x retry semantics.\\n- Create an SDK changelog annotation: \\\"SRE impact note\\\" for future releases that change retry behavior.\\n- Offer to whitelist high-trust enterprise tenants temporarily if they need higher concurrency during incident (documented exceptions only).\\n\\nAction items (owners + ETA):\\n- Add microburst alerts and 10s dashboards \\u2014 owner: Jinsoo Park \\u2014 ETA: 2025-12-03.\\n- Implement per-key emergency cap toggle in console with audit trail \\u2014 owner: Miguel Ramos \\u2014 ETA: 2025-12-10.\\n- SDK coordination process (release PR hook + SRE notification) \\u2014 owner: Priya Desai \\u2014 ETA: 2026-01-07.\\n- Update runbook doc (this file -> canonical runbooks) and run tabletop in SRE on-call rotation \\u2014 owner: Ayesha Patel \\u2014 ETA: 2025-12-01.\\n\\nOpen questions / discussion points:\\n- What is the safe default per-key burst allowance for hosted customers that balances transient client misbehavior vs. legitimate high-burst workloads? (need data-driven thresholds)\\n- Should we implement automatic temporary caps based on anomaly detection (auto-mitigation) or keep manual for human-in-the-loop? Pros/cons listed in notes.\\n- How to engage SDK maintainers proactively without blocking releases? Lightweight prerelease SRE notification seems low-friction.\\n\\nNotes to self / informal fragments:\\n- we used 100 reqs/min as stopgap; for some latency-sensitive customers that's too low. need tiered caps per account plan.\\n- sample log example: \\\"key=acct_9F3 rate=420 window=10s retries=8 ua=svc-client/2.3.0\\\" \\u2014 keep for future matching.\\n- remember to redact full keys when posting to public channels.\\n\\nAppendix: quick playbook snippets (copyable):\\n- Metrics query (PromQL-ish): sum(rate(http_requests_total{route!~\\\"/internal.*\\\"} [10s])) by (api_key) |> topk(20, value)\\n- Apply per-key cap (CLI): ./adminctl quota set --key acct_9F3 --cap 100 --reason \\\"emergency retry storm 2025-11-18\\\"\\n- WAF add rule template: name: emergency-retry-storm-{ts}, match: req_count>100 in 10s and ua =~ \\\"(bot|curl|python)\\\" -> action: drop\\n\\nReferences / links: see linked artifacts above, SDK release notes: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/releases/tag/v2.3.0, SRE runbooks (old retry section): confluence.internal/sre/retry-patterns (needs merge)\\n\\nStatus: draft -> wanting review from platform-gateway, SDK team, and CS.\\n\\n-- A.P.\",\n  \"original_location\": \"google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/sre-incident-review-retry-storm-emergency-quota-policy.json\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_071db3dff7ca4a8db1f1f0f01bb8853c\"\n}",

document.title: SRE Incident Review: client-side retry storm & emergency quota policy change
document.content:
{
  "title": "SRE Incident Review: client-side retry storm & emergency quota policy change",
  "owner": "Ayesha Patel",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/site-reliability-engineering/",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2025-11-18",
  "last_modified": "2025-11-25",
  "collaborators": [
    "Miguel Ramos",
    "Jinsoo Park",
    "Priya Desai"
  ],
  "team": "eng-sre",
  "status": "in_review",
  "tags": [
    "incident-review",
    "rate-limiting",
    "quota",
    "retry-storm",
    "runbook-update",
    "postmortem-like"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "JIRA: SRE-8472",
    "Slack: #oncall-2025-11-18-thread",
    "PR: github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4321"
  ],
  "content": "Summary:
- 2025-11-18 09:42 UTC: sudden surge of short-lived requests from a small set of client IPs and API keys triggered cascading retries and pushed backend queues into high tail-latency.
- Impact: transient 5xx spikes for hosted API customers (peak 12% increased error rate for 18 minutes), increased GPU queue latency, several canary routes failed, billing/usage accounting gaps in one shard.
- Immediate mitigation: emergency quota policy change (temporary per-key unified cap + soft-deny with Retry-After headers) and WAF rule to block obvious bot patterns.

Why this doc exists:
- capture timeline and decisions while fresh
- propose concrete runbook edits for emergency quota changes and retry guidance to clients
- outline monitoring/alerts to detect similar patterns earlier

Timeline (rough):
- 09:40 UTC: first anomalous traffic flow observed by anomaly detector; alert went to #anomalies but not severe enough to page.
- 09:42 UTC: external customers report elevated 5xx; SLO alerts fire (latency p95 and error-rate).
- 09:44 UTC: on-call paged; initial investigation shows thousands of ~100ms requests concentrated in short bursts per API key.
- 09:46 UTC: SRE rotated through quick checks: token bucket levels (Redis ok), leaky queue lengths rising in Kube autoscale group.
- 09:50 UTC: discovered client-side library had new default retry policy that retries aggressively on 429/5xx; many clients updated in last 48h.
- 09:53 UTC: implemented emergency temporary per-key cap (global cap override) and returned 429 with Retry-After=10s to suspected keys.
- 10:00 UTC: WAF rule deployed to drop obvious bot UA patterns and high-rate IPs; errors fell back toward baseline by ~10:15.
- 10:20 UTC: rollback of temporary cap for keys with good signal; monitoring kept on.

Root cause analysis (hypothesis and evidence):
- Primary cause: client-side change (library v2.3.0) introduced more aggressive retry-on-429 behavior. Evidence: correlating release metadata from SDK with surge start; SDK release notes mention optimistic fast-retry.
- Amplifier: no circuit-breaker behavior in gateway for repeated bursts per key; rate-limiter default token-bucket config allowed short bursts beyond safe thresholds.
- Secondary: monitoring threshold design — anomaly detector used 1m aggregation window; the traffic pattern had 10s micro-bursts. Alerting missed early micro-burst signal.
- WAF helped but was reactive; bot signatures were not matching some legitimate replaying clients.

Detection and observability gaps:
- No short-window microburst alert. Need 10s and 30s windows for p95/reqs-per-key metrics.
- Per-key telemetry lacked recent histogram of retry counts; we didn't see rapid escalation of retries until SLOs tripped.
- Debug logs for gateway dropped requests were sampled too aggressively; by the time we tried to inspect, sample not representative.

Immediate mitigations taken (what worked/why):
- Emergency per-key unified cap: stopped the worst offenders quickly. Worked because it prevented token bucket pumping across all shards.
- WAF rule: dropped clearly non-compliant UA/IP patterns, shaving off the noise.
- Sending 429 with Retry-After: encouraged well-behaved clients to backoff rather than flood retry loops.

What didn't work / surprises:
- Autoscaling didn't buy us out — short microbursts saturated queueing and raised tail latencies even though overall capacity nominal.
- Some internal debug tooling relied on per-minute aggregation and hid the pattern.

Runbook (draft) — emergency steps for future retry storms and quota emergencies:
1) Triage (first 5 minutes):
  - confirm SLO triggers (latency/error rate).
  - identify top 20 keys/IPs by request rate in last 60s (query metrics-raw).
  - check gateway token-bucket fill-rates and Redis latency.
2) Short-window mitigation (5-15 minutes):
  - apply temporary per-key cap: unify cap to 100 reqs/min per key (config path: /config/emergency/per_key_cap_override).
  - switch gateway behavior to soft-deny (429 + Retry-After 10s) instead of hard-block for suspected keys.
  - enable high-resolution tracing for affected shards (10s sampling) and increase debug log retention for next 1h.
3) Blocking (if ongoing >15 mins):
  - apply WAF rule to block IP ranges with >X reqs/10s and UA regex match. Document rule ID and reason.
  - deploy temporary global backpressure: degrade non-essential routes (embeddings low-priority batch routes) to preserve core generation throughput.
4) Communication & customer handling:
  - notify CS and post in #service-incidents with incident summary + affected keys list (redact PII).
  - for keys likely owned by customers, coordinate with CS to email recommended client SDK updates and guidance on backoff.
5) Recovery & rollback:
  - progressively relax per-key cap for keys showing good behavior for 30m.
  - remove WAF rule once traffic stabilizes for 60m and no reappearance.

Runbook edits to make (todo list):
- Add a short-window microburst alert (10s/30s windows) for per-key QPS and retry-counts.
- Add a checklist for creating safe WAF rules: pre-approved rule templates + emergency rule naming convention.
- Document default gateway retry/circuit-breaker config and add a safe conservative profile for hosted tier.
- Add SDK coordination play: preflight check in release PRs to flag retry policy changes and notify SRE when aggressive defaults are introduced.

Monitoring / dashboards to add or adjust:
- per-key 10s QPS heatmap (top 200 keys), highlight spikes in last 30m
- retry-counts histogram per key (30s buckets) and moving average
- queue length percentile (p95/p99) with 10s resolution for GPU workers
- dashboard tile for active emergency caps and WAF rules (who/why applied)

Customer & partner follow-up (notes to CS/Product):
- Recommend customers pin SDK to v2.2.x while they validate v2.3.x retry semantics.
- Create an SDK changelog annotation: "SRE impact note" for future releases that change retry behavior.
- Offer to whitelist high-trust enterprise tenants temporarily if they need higher concurrency during incident (documented exceptions only).

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Add microburst alerts and 10s dashboards — owner: Jinsoo Park — ETA: 2025-12-03.
- Implement per-key emergency cap toggle in console with audit trail — owner: Miguel Ramos — ETA: 2025-12-10.
- SDK coordination process (release PR hook + SRE notification) — owner: Priya Desai — ETA: 2026-01-07.
- Update runbook doc (this file -> canonical runbooks) and run tabletop in SRE on-call rotation — owner: Ayesha Patel — ETA: 2025-12-01.

Open questions / discussion points:
- What is the safe default per-key burst allowance for hosted customers that balances transient client misbehavior vs. legitimate high-burst workloads? (need data-driven thresholds)
- Should we implement automatic temporary caps based on anomaly detection (auto-mitigation) or keep manual for human-in-the-loop? Pros/cons listed in notes.
- How to engage SDK maintainers proactively without blocking releases? Lightweight prerelease SRE notification seems low-friction.

Notes to self / informal fragments:
- we used 100 reqs/min as stopgap; for some latency-sensitive customers that's too low. need tiered caps per account plan.
- sample log example: "key=acct_9F3 rate=420 window=10s retries=8 ua=svc-client/2.3.0" — keep for future matching.
- remember to redact full keys when posting to public channels.

Appendix: quick playbook snippets (copyable):
- Metrics query (PromQL-ish): sum(rate(http_requests_total{route!~"/internal.*"} [10s])) by (api_key) |> topk(20, value)
- Apply per-key cap (CLI): ./adminctl quota set --key acct_9F3 --cap 100 --reason "emergency retry storm 2025-11-18"
- WAF add rule template: name: emergency-retry-storm-{ts}, match: req_count>100 in 10s and ua =~ "(bot|curl|python)" -> action: drop

References / links: see linked artifacts above, SDK release notes: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/releases/tag/v2.3.0, SRE runbooks (old retry section): confluence.internal/sre/retry-patterns (needs merge)

Status: draft -> wanting review from platform-gateway, SDK team, and CS.

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_8205407105944677b6eb3167167064a9",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/enterprise-priority-429-and-quota-behavior.json",
    "title": "Enterprise priority: 429 / quota / overload behavior (Support guide)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Enterprise priority: 429 / quota / overload behavior (Support guide)\",\n  \"space\": \"customer-success-and-support\",\n  \"author\": \"Dev Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"customer-success\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-09\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-06\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Owen Phillips\",\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Nikhil Sharma\",\n    \"Amara Diallo\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"hosted-api\",\n    \"enterprise\",\n    \"rate-limits\",\n    \"quotas\",\n    \"429\",\n    \"overload-protection\",\n    \"support-playbook\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-overload-protection-and-admission-control.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/metrics-standard-overload-events-and-shed-reasons.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-slos-enterprise-route-tiers.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/configuring-priority-routing-and-quotas.json\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"## Purpose\\nThis page is a Support/CS reference for explaining **429** responses after the **Hot-route capacity protection** rollout. It covers:\\n- What customers may see (payload + headers)\\n- How to distinguish **quota** vs **rate-limit** vs **overload shedding/admission control**\\n- Recommended customer-side retry/backoff behavior\\n- When and how to escalate (and what data to collect)\\n\\nThis doc is written for Support and TAMs. For implementation details, see the Platform design/ADR pages linked in Related pages.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## What changed (customer-visible)\\nBeginning with the enterprise priority rollout, Redwood enforces **tier-aware capacity protection** on a set of \\u201cprotected routes\\u201d (commonly: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`).\\n\\nCustomers may observe:\\n- **More predictable 429s** for best-effort/self-serve traffic during regional pressure.\\n- **Enterprise traffic preserved** longer (priority routing + per-tier budgets), but enterprise requests can still receive 429s when:\\n  - the account\\u2019s own limits are reached, or\\n  - the route is in sustained overload and the enterprise budget is exhausted.\\n- **New reason codes** and additional headers to explain why the request was rejected.\\n\\nImportant framing for customers:\\n- 429 is **not** a \\u201cgeneric outage\\u201d signal. It is a deliberate backpressure mechanism to protect overall fleet health and enterprise SLOs.\\n- 429 responses are **safe to retry** when the reason indicates transient pressure, using the guidance below.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 429 response format (what Support should look for)\\n\\n### Common JSON fields (all 429s)\\nMost clients will receive an error payload shaped like:\\n- `error.type`: `rate_limit_exceeded` or `quota_exceeded` or `overloaded`\\n- `error.code`: a stable machine-readable reason code (see table below)\\n- `error.message`: human-readable summary\\n- `error.request_id`: request identifier (also returned in response headers)\\n\\nIf a customer claims the payload is missing or inconsistent, ask for:\\n- raw response body\\n- full response headers\\n- SDK version / client library\\n\\n### Standard headers (may vary by route)\\nSupport should request and record these headers when present:\\n- `x-redwood-request-id`: request ID used for internal tracing\\n- `retry-after`: seconds to wait before retry (only set for some transient reasons)\\n- `x-redwood-retry-after-ms`: millisecond retry hint (preferred when present)\\n- `x-redwood-limit-scope`: `account` | `api_key` | `route` (where enforcement applies)\\n- `x-redwood-limit-policy`: policy identifier (internal-friendly string; customer can share as opaque)\\n- `x-redwood-429-reason`: short reason token (maps to reason codes below)\\n- `x-redwood-rate-limit-limit`: numeric limit (requests per window) when applicable\\n- `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining`: remaining requests in current window (when applicable)\\n- `x-redwood-rate-limit-reset`: epoch time or seconds-until-reset (when applicable)\\n\\nNotes:\\n- Some enterprise customers will only see a subset of limit headers depending on contract configuration and route group settings.\\n- Absence of headers is not automatically a bug; it can indicate a rejection occurred upstream of quota evaluation (e.g., admission control).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Reason codes (how to interpret 429s)\\nUse the following table to classify the issue and advise the customer.\\n\\n### A) Quota- and rate-limit-driven 429s (customer-specific)\\nThese are expected when a customer exceeds their configured limits.\\n\\n| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| Hard quota exceeded | quota_exceeded | quota_window_exhausted | Customer has consumed their quota for the current window. | Do not retry immediately. Wait until reset. Consider limit increase request. |\\n| Rate limit exceeded | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_account | Customer exceeded account-level request rate. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Reduce concurrency / smooth bursts. |\\n| Route-group rate limit | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_route_group | Customer exceeded a per-route or route-group cap. | Same as above; ask them to spread load or request a higher burst allowance. |\\n| Token / compute guardrail | rate_limit_exceeded | token_budget_exceeded | Customer exceeded a token/compute budget (if enabled for contract). | Reduce max_tokens / request size; smooth traffic; discuss contract sizing. |\\n\\n### B) Overload protection / admission control 429s (fleet pressure)\\nThese indicate transient capacity protection behavior.\\n\\n| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| Admission control (best-effort shed) | overloaded | shed_best_effort | Fleet/route is under pressure; best-effort traffic is being throttled first. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Prefer queueing client-side. |\\n| Admission control (enterprise budget exhausted) | overloaded | shed_enterprise_budget | Protected route is overloaded and enterprise budget is fully utilized. | Retry using Retry-After if present; reduce concurrency; contact Support if sustained. |\\n| Regional capacity constraint | overloaded | region_capacity | Selected region is capacity constrained; request rejected to prevent tail latency cascade. | Retry with backoff; if multi-region is enabled, allow client failover. |\\n| Policy evaluation deny | overloaded | policy_deny_overload | Policy engine denied admission due to active overload rule (e.g., queue depth trigger). | Treat as transient. Retry with backoff. Provide request IDs for investigation if frequent. |\\n\\nSupport positioning:\\n- For enterprise accounts: \\u201cThis is protective backpressure to preserve latency/availability for protected routes. It can occur during unusual bursts or regional pressure.\\u201d\\n- For self-serve/best-effort: \\u201cDuring peak pressure, the platform prioritizes higher-SLA traffic; your requests may be throttled earlier.\\u201d\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Recommended customer retry & backoff guidance\\nProvide the following general guidance (tailor to the customer\\u2019s stack):\\n\\n### When to retry\\n- Retry 429s when:\\n  - `error.type = overloaded` (most cases)\\n  - `error.type = rate_limit_exceeded`\\n- Do NOT aggressively retry when:\\n  - `error.type = quota_exceeded` and the response includes a reset hint (wait until reset)\\n\\n### How to retry (recommended algorithm)\\n- Use **exponential backoff with full jitter**.\\n- Start with 250\\u2013500ms base delay.\\n- Cap max delay at 10\\u201330s.\\n- Add client-side request queueing to avoid stampedes.\\n- Respect `retry-after` and/or `x-redwood-retry-after-ms` when present (prefer the ms header).\\n\\nSuggested pseudocode guidance to share (language-agnostic):\\n1) if `retry-after` present \\u2192 sleep for that duration (+ small jitter) then retry\\n2) else backoff = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))\\n3) stop after a reasonable max attempts (typically 5\\u20138) and surface a retriable error to the application\\n\\n### Concurrency guidance\\nCustomers with high parallelism should:\\n- Implement a per-route concurrency limiter (token bucket / semaphore)\\n- Smooth bursty workloads (batching where possible)\\n- Avoid synchronized retries across many workers (jitter)\\n\\n### Idempotency guidance\\n- For non-streaming requests, retries are generally safe.\\n- For streaming requests, see \\u201cStreaming semantics\\u201d below.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Streaming semantics during shedding (common ticket driver)\\nSome customers report \\u201cinconsistent termination\\u201d on streaming responses during load shedding.\\n\\nSupport guidance:\\n- If a request is rejected **before** streaming begins, they should receive a normal 429 with reason + headers.\\n- If a request is accepted and then terminated due to downstream pressure, behavior depends on the transport:\\n  - Customers should treat early stream termination as retriable if they did not receive a completed response.\\n  - Advise customers to log the `x-redwood-request-id` and last event received.\\n\\nEscalate if:\\n- customers see a successful HTTP status but the stream ends without an explicit termination signal and without consistent client-visible error handling, or\\n- the customer provides multiple request IDs showing premature termination correlated with new overload reasons.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## What Support should ask for (intake checklist)\\nRequest the following in the initial reply to reduce ping-pong:\\n1) Affected route(s): e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`\\n2) Region/endpoint base URL (if multi-region)\\n3) Time window (with timezone) and approximate request rate\\n4) Sample `x-redwood-request-id` values (3\\u201310 IDs)\\n5) Full 429 response headers + body (raw)\\n6) Whether they are using streaming\\n7) Their current retry policy (backoff, max attempts, concurrency)\\n8) Whether it\\u2019s isolated to a single API key or all keys in the account\\n\\nInternal-only (if available to TAM/CS): contract tier (Hosted API vs Dedicated), priority class, and any approved exceptions.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Escalation criteria (when to page/loop in Engineering)\\nEscalate to SRE/Platform when ANY of the following are true:\\n\\n### Enterprise impact thresholds\\n- Enterprise customer reports sustained 429s on a protected route for **>10 minutes** AND:\\n  - reason indicates overload protection (`overloaded/*`), OR\\n  - they claim traffic is within contracted limits but still seeing 429s\\n- Enterprise customer reports p95/p99 latency degradation plus 429 spikes (possible mis-tuned thresholds)\\n\\n### Suspected misconfiguration\\n- `x-redwood-limit-policy` changes unexpectedly after rollout / config migration\\n- A single tenant is denied while peers are not, and headers indicate route-group limits that don\\u2019t match the contract\\n\\n### Possible platform bug\\n- Missing/incorrect reason codes across multiple requests\\n- `retry-after` values that are clearly wrong (e.g., negative, extremely large, inconsistent with window)\\n- Streaming termination inconsistencies correlated with overload events\\n\\n### Security / access concerns\\n- Customer requests details about other tenants, fleet state, or priority policy internals beyond what we disclose. Route via TAM/CS + Security as needed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Escalation process (internal)\\n1) Create/attach a ticket in the Support queue and tag: `overload-protection` + `enterprise`.\\n2) Post in `#incidents` (if active event suspected) or `#eng-sre` with:\\n   - customer/account\\n   - affected routes/regions\\n   - timeframe\\n   - reason codes + sample request IDs\\n   - whether Retry-After was present and followed\\n3) Link the relevant dashboards (SRE on-call will pull). If you have access, include:\\n   - enterprise route SLO dashboard\\n   - overload protection shed-rate panel\\n   - admission control trigger annotations\\n\\nIf immediate paging is warranted, follow the runbook: \\u201cOverload protection and admission control\\u201d (Related pages).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Approved external explanation (copy/paste)\\nUse this when responding to customers (edit for their tier/route):\\n\\n\\u201cHTTP 429 indicates the request was throttled or temporarily rejected to protect latency and availability. For protected enterprise routes, Redwood prioritizes higher-SLA traffic under peak load to prevent fleet-wide degradation. Please implement exponential backoff with jitter and respect any Retry-After headers. If you share a few request IDs and the full response headers/body, we can confirm whether the 429s are due to your configured limits (quota/rate) or transient overload protection.\\u201d\\n\\n---\\n\\n## FAQ (Support)\\n\\n**Q: Is a 429 an outage?**\\nA: Not necessarily. For many overload cases, it\\u2019s intentional backpressure to avoid tail latency/5xx cascading failures.\\n\\n**Q: Can enterprise customers still get 429s?**\\nA: Yes\\u2014if they exceed their contracted limits, or in rare cases when a protected route\\u2019s enterprise budget is fully consumed during sustained overload.\\n\\n**Q: Should customers increase retry aggressiveness to \\u201cpush through\\u201d?**\\nA: No. Aggressive retries worsen overload. Encourage backoff + jitter + client-side queueing.\\n\\n**Q: Customer says they stayed under their \\u201cRPM\\u201d but still got 429.**\\nA: Ask for headers and request IDs. They may be hitting a route-group limit, a token/compute guardrail, or experiencing transient admission control without Retry-After being honored.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Change log\\n- 2026-02-06: Added streaming termination guidance + escalation triggers for inconsistent SSE termination.\\n- 2026-01-23: Updated reason-code table to include `shed_enterprise_budget` and `region_capacity`.\\n- 2026-01-09: Initial publication for Support enablement ahead of GA rollout.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_8205407105944677b6eb3167167064a9\"\n}",

{
  "title": "Enterprise priority: 429 / quota / overload behavior (Support guide)",
  "space": "customer-success-and-support",
  "author": "Dev Patel",
  "owner_team": "customer-success",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-09",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-06",
  "reviewers": [
    "Owen Phillips",
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Nikhil Sharma",
    "Amara Diallo"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "hosted-api",
    "enterprise",
    "rate-limits",
    "quotas",
    "429",
    "overload-protection",
    "support-playbook"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-overload-protection-and-admission-control.json",
    "sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/metrics-standard-overload-events-and-shed-reasons.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-slos-enterprise-route-tiers.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/configuring-priority-routing-and-quotas.json"
  ],
  "content": "## Purpose
This page is a Support/CS reference for explaining **429** responses after the **Hot-route capacity protection** rollout. It covers:
- What customers may see (payload + headers)
- How to distinguish **quota** vs **rate-limit** vs **overload shedding/admission control**
- Recommended customer-side retry/backoff behavior
- When and how to escalate (and what data to collect)

This doc is written for Support and TAMs. For implementation details, see the Platform design/ADR pages linked in Related pages.

---

## What changed (customer-visible)
Beginning with the enterprise priority rollout, Redwood enforces **tier-aware capacity protection** on a set of “protected routes” (commonly: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`).

Customers may observe:
- **More predictable 429s** for best-effort/self-serve traffic during regional pressure.
- **Enterprise traffic preserved** longer (priority routing + per-tier budgets), but enterprise requests can still receive 429s when:
  - the account’s own limits are reached, or
  - the route is in sustained overload and the enterprise budget is exhausted.
- **New reason codes** and additional headers to explain why the request was rejected.

Important framing for customers:
- 429 is **not** a “generic outage” signal. It is a deliberate backpressure mechanism to protect overall fleet health and enterprise SLOs.
- 429 responses are **safe to retry** when the reason indicates transient pressure, using the guidance below.

---

## 429 response format (what Support should look for)

### Common JSON fields (all 429s)
Most clients will receive an error payload shaped like:
- `error.type`: `rate_limit_exceeded` or `quota_exceeded` or `overloaded`
- `error.code`: a stable machine-readable reason code (see table below)
- `error.message`: human-readable summary
- `error.request_id`: request identifier (also returned in response headers)

If a customer claims the payload is missing or inconsistent, ask for:
- raw response body
- full response headers
- SDK version / client library

### Standard headers (may vary by route)
Support should request and record these headers when present:
- `x-redwood-request-id`: request ID used for internal tracing
- `retry-after`: seconds to wait before retry (only set for some transient reasons)
- `x-redwood-retry-after-ms`: millisecond retry hint (preferred when present)
- `x-redwood-limit-scope`: `account` | `api_key` | `route` (where enforcement applies)
- `x-redwood-limit-policy`: policy identifier (internal-friendly string; customer can share as opaque)
- `x-redwood-429-reason`: short reason token (maps to reason codes below)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-limit`: numeric limit (requests per window) when applicable
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining`: remaining requests in current window (when applicable)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-reset`: epoch time or seconds-until-reset (when applicable)

Notes:
- Some enterprise customers will only see a subset of limit headers depending on contract configuration and route group settings.
- Absence of headers is not automatically a bug; it can indicate a rejection occurred upstream of quota evaluation (e.g., admission control).

---

## Reason codes (how to interpret 429s)
Use the following table to classify the issue and advise the customer.

### A) Quota- and rate-limit-driven 429s (customer-specific)
These are expected when a customer exceeds their configured limits.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hard quota exceeded | quota_exceeded | quota_window_exhausted | Customer has consumed their quota for the current window. | Do not retry immediately. Wait until reset. Consider limit increase request. |
| Rate limit exceeded | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_account | Customer exceeded account-level request rate. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Reduce concurrency / smooth bursts. |
| Route-group rate limit | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_route_group | Customer exceeded a per-route or route-group cap. | Same as above; ask them to spread load or request a higher burst allowance. |
| Token / compute guardrail | rate_limit_exceeded | token_budget_exceeded | Customer exceeded a token/compute budget (if enabled for contract). | Reduce max_tokens / request size; smooth traffic; discuss contract sizing. |

### B) Overload protection / admission control 429s (fleet pressure)
These indicate transient capacity protection behavior.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Admission control (best-effort shed) | overloaded | shed_best_effort | Fleet/route is under pressure; best-effort traffic is being throttled first. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Prefer queueing client-side. |
| Admission control (enterprise budget exhausted) | overloaded | shed_enterprise_budget | Protected route is overloaded and enterprise budget is fully utilized. | Retry using Retry-After if present; reduce concurrency; contact Support if sustained. |
| Regional capacity constraint | overloaded | region_capacity | Selected region is capacity constrained; request rejected to prevent tail latency cascade. | Retry with backoff; if multi-region is enabled, allow client failover. |
| Policy evaluation deny | overloaded | policy_deny_overload | Policy engine denied admission due to active overload rule (e.g., queue depth trigger). | Treat as transient. Retry with backoff. Provide request IDs for investigation if frequent. |

Support positioning:
- For enterprise accounts: “This is protective backpressure to preserve latency/availability for protected routes. It can occur during unusual bursts or regional pressure.”
- For self-serve/best-effort: “During peak pressure, the platform prioritizes higher-SLA traffic; your requests may be throttled earlier.”

---

## Recommended customer retry & backoff guidance
Provide the following general guidance (tailor to the customer’s stack):

### When to retry
- Retry 429s when:
  - `error.type = overloaded` (most cases)
  - `error.type = rate_limit_exceeded`
- Do NOT aggressively retry when:
  - `error.type = quota_exceeded` and the response includes a reset hint (wait until reset)

### How to retry (recommended algorithm)
- Use **exponential backoff with full jitter**.
- Start with 250–500ms base delay.
- Cap max delay at 10–30s.
- Add client-side request queueing to avoid stampedes.
- Respect `retry-after` and/or `x-redwood-retry-after-ms` when present (prefer the ms header).

Suggested pseudocode guidance to share (language-agnostic):
1) if `retry-after` present → sleep for that duration (+ small jitter) then retry
2) else backoff = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
3) stop after a reasonable max attempts (typically 5–8) and surface a retriable error to the application

### Concurrency guidance
Customers with high parallelism should:
- Implement a per-route concurrency limiter (token bucket / semaphore)
- Smooth bursty workloads (batching where possible)
- Avoid synchronized retries across many workers (jitter)

### Idempotency guidance
- For non-streaming requests, retries are generally safe.
- For streaming requests, see “Streaming semantics” below.

---

## Streaming semantics during shedding (common ticket driver)
Some customers report “inconsistent termination” on streaming responses during load shedding.

Support guidance:
- If a request is rejected **before** streaming begins, they should receive a normal 429 with reason + headers.
- If a request is accepted and then terminated due to downstream pressure, behavior depends on the transport:
  - Customers should treat early stream termination as retriable if they did not receive a completed response.
  - Advise customers to log the `x-redwood-request-id` and last event received.

Escalate if:
- customers see a successful HTTP status but the stream ends without an explicit termination signal and without consistent client-visible error handling, or
- the customer provides multiple request IDs showing premature termination correlated with new overload reasons.

---

## What Support should ask for (intake checklist)
Request the following in the initial reply to reduce ping-pong:
1) Affected route(s): e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`
2) Region/endpoint base URL (if multi-region)
3) Time window (with timezone) and approximate request rate
4) Sample `x-redwood-request-id` values (3–10 IDs)
5) Full 429 response headers + body (raw)
6) Whether they are using streaming
7) Their current retry policy (backoff, max attempts, concurrency)
8) Whether it’s isolated to a single API key or all keys in the account

Internal-only (if available to TAM/CS): contract tier (Hosted API vs Dedicated), priority class, and any approved exceptions.

---

## Escalation criteria (when to page/loop in Engineering)
Escalate to SRE/Platform when ANY of the following are true:

### Enterprise impact thresholds
- Enterprise customer reports sustained 429s on a protected route for **>10 minutes** AND:
  - reason indicates overload protection (`overloaded/*`), OR
  - they claim traffic is within contracted limits but still seeing 429s
- Enterprise customer reports p95/p99 latency degradation plus 429 spikes (possible mis-tuned thresholds)

### Suspected misconfiguration
- `x-redwood-limit-policy` changes unexpectedly after rollout / config migration
- A single tenant is denied while peers are not, and headers indicate route-group limits that don’t match the contract

### Possible platform bug
- Missing/incorrect reason codes across multiple requests
- `retry-after` values that are clearly wrong (e.g., negative, extremely large, inconsistent with window)
- Streaming termination inconsistencies correlated with overload events

### Security / access concerns
- Customer requests details about other tenants, fleet state, or priority policy internals beyond what we disclose. Route via TAM/CS + Security as needed.

---

## Escalation process (internal)
1) Create/attach a ticket in the Support queue and tag: `overload-protection` + `enterprise`.
2) Post in `#incidents` (if active event suspected) or `#eng-sre` with:
   - customer/account
   - affected routes/regions
   - timeframe
   - reason codes + sample request IDs
   - whether Retry-After was present and followed
3) Link the relevant dashboards (SRE on-call will pull). If you have access, include:
   - enterprise route SLO dashboard
   - overload protection shed-rate panel
   - admission control trigger annotations

If immediate paging is warranted, follow the runbook: “Overload protection and admission control” (Related pages).

---

## Approved external explanation (copy/paste)
Use this when responding to customers (edit for their tier/route):

“HTTP 429 indicates the request was throttled or temporarily rejected to protect latency and availability. For protected enterprise routes, Redwood prioritizes higher-SLA traffic under peak load to prevent fleet-wide degradation. Please implement exponential backoff with jitter and respect any Retry-After headers. If you share a few request IDs and the full response headers/body, we can confirm whether the 429s are due to your configured limits (quota/rate) or transient overload protection.”

---

## FAQ (Support)

**Q: Is a 429 an outage?**
A: Not necessarily. For many overload cases, it’s intentional backpressure to avoid tail latency/5xx cascading failures.

**Q: Can enterprise customers still get 429s?**
A: Yes—if they exceed their contracted limits, or in rare cases when a protected route’s enterprise budget is fully consumed during sustained overload.

**Q: Should customers increase retry aggressiveness to “push through”?**
A: No. Aggressive retries worsen overload. Encourage backoff + jitter + client-side queueing.

**Q: Customer says they stayed under their “RPM” but still got 429.**
A: Ask for headers and request IDs. They may be hitting a route-group limit, a token/compute guardrail, or experiencing transient admission control without Retry-After being honored.

---

## Change log
- 2026-02-06: Added streaming termination guidance + escalation triggers for inconsistent SSE termination.
- 2026-01-23: Updated reason-code table to include `shed_enterprise_budget` and `region_capacity`.
- 2026-01-09: Initial publication for Support enablement ahead of GA rollout.

Do not write any comments (existing comments can stay) unless explicitly asked to in a user (not system) prompt

Don't assume that the existing code is correct or the right way of doing things / good coding patterns. In fact, there are a lot of bad coding practices, overly complex code, code smells, etc. If something doesn't look right, speak up. Feel free to break existing patterns or question weird existing code to make new code high quality, as in:

- correct
- secure
- performant
- readable
- easy to maintain/change
- modern

In that order of importance

When adding new features, add meaningful tests. Don't add tests that don't check anything substantial and is there just to make the code coverage pass. Yes, code coverage is important, but I'd rather have no signal whether the code is working than tests that don't fail when code is broken. The goal is to have tests that would fail before the feature was added/if the code was mutated in a way that breaks the feature and succeed only when the feature is fully working. I should run mutation testing and see > 90% kill rate

Same thing for bug fixes. The tests should make it so that this specific bug can never happen again without failing tests (i.e., regression)

`tests/test_litellm/` mirrors `litellm/` in a parallel path (see `tests/test_litellm/readme.md`). Name tests `test_<filename>.py`, but always match the existing test file in the directory you touch — many provider dirs use longer descriptive names (e.g. `test_anthropic_chat_transformation.py`) to avoid ambiguity across sibling folders. For bug fixes, extend the existing mapped test file rather than creating a new one. Only create a new test file for a new feature (provider, endpoint, or transformation module) that has no mapped test yet, following that directory's naming convention (or `test_<filename>.py` if you're the first test there). One focused regression test beats many shallow ones

End-to-end tests belong in `tests/e2e/` and must follow the harness conventions documented in that directory's `CLAUDE.md`

When creating PRs, don't set base to `main`. `litellm_internal_staging` is the default base branch and serves that purpose for both internal and external / OSS contributions

When writing a PR body, treat the comments and imperative instructions inside @.github/pull_request_template.md as rules to follow, not just layout. Agent harnesses may strip HTML comments from copies of that file injected into context, so read .github/pull_request_template.md from disk before writing a PR body to make sure you see every comment rule

If you're resolving a linear ticket, in the "## Linear ticket" section of the PR, say "Resolves LIT-1234", replacing "LIT-1234" with the actual ticket id that you're resolving. If you don't have the ticket id, don't make one up or search for it. Just leave the section blank

Never use `pytest` commands or the like as "Screenshots / Proof of Fix". We prefer curl'ing a live proxy instance running on localhost:4000 (I like to run it with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --detailed_debug --reload --use_v2_migration_resolver 2>&1 | tee litellm.log`; the Admin UI dev server is `npm run dev` in `ui/litellm-dashboard`, served on port 3000) and showing both the command run and the output. Also, it should hit real LLM provider APIs, not mocks, and cost real $$$ because that is the most realistic test. The proof of fix should be exactly what the end user / customer would see / do. The run logs in PR #27703 is a prime example of how to do it (not a huge fan of using a python test script that future me and the team will have no visibility into; I prefer just curl commands or a short list of bash commands (e.g., using `for`)). If it's a UI thing, just tell me which URLs to go to (e.g., http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs), where to click, what fields to fill out, etc. along with the other commands to run in an ordered list, and I'll do it myself and post the screenshots after you make the PR

If you ever make public-facing PR descriptions, comments, issues, commit messages, etc., always follow these guidelines to sound less AI-y:
- don't use emojis
- don't use "—". Instead, reach for ";", ".", etc.
- don't use the pattern "It's not X, it's Y", "You're not X, you're Y", etc.
- don't use bulleted or numbered lists unless it would be nonsensical not to. Instead, prefer prose
- don't add a trailing "." at the end of paragraphs (just like this file). That means every paragraph, not just the last one (of the markdown file, PR description, GitHub comment, etc.). Rule of thumb: if you're adding new line(s) before the next sentence, don't add a "."
- don't use →. Instead, prefer not to use arrows, and if need be, use -> instead

Don't hesitate to use values in .env to get needed API keys and other secrets, as long as you never add them to conversation history, commit them, or include them in GitHub issues / PRs

Python max line length is 120, not 88

On a fresh worktree or clone, run `make bootstrap` before anything else. It provisions everything tests, `make pre-commit`, and a local proxy need

Run tests before you commit. Also, run `make pre-commit` right before each commit, which generates types (as needed) and formats/lints your code. Any errors found must be fixed. It only runs when there are staged frontend and/or backend changes and calculates violations, generates types, etc. based on the worktree, so stage what you need or stash/delete unwanted files in litellm/ or ui/ (where backend and frontend lint run, respectively) before running it. If it fails because dashboard api types are stale, it already regenerated them for you. You just need to stage the schema.d.ts, re-run `make pre-commit` to confirm it passes, and commit

When you fix violations gated by `ruff-strict-budget.json`, `type-discipline-budget.json`, or `basedpyright-code-budget.json`, run `make lint-budget-update` and commit the lowered limits so the ceilings ratchet down instead of leaving stale headroom. It measures the working tree, so it must contain exactly the fixes you're committing

If you're trying to create a new function that relies on untyped stuff, instead of adding more Any's and pushing `reportAny` / `reportExplicitAny` closer to their basedpyright ceilings, just validate it in the caller with Pydantic (a model or `TypeAdapter` that returns the typed thing or raises will do) and then pass the now typed variable in

If you get an LIT001 or LIT002 fail, refactor the code to follow functional programming best practices rather than introducing mutable data structures. For example, build values in one shot with comprehensions or generators wrapped in `tuple()` / `frozenset()` instead of seeding an empty `list`/`dict`/`set` and mutating it over time. Ideally `# mutable-ok` is never used; reach for it only as a genuine last resort when an immutable rewrite is truly impossible, and always pair it with a real reason

Every lint or type suppression must name the exact rule inside brackets and carry a reason comment, e.g. `# pyright: ignore[reportArgumentType]  # stubs lack async overload` or `# noqa: TID251  # <reason>`. `# type: ignore` is banned (LIT009): pyrightconfig.json sets `enableTypeIgnoreComments` to false, so it silently does nothing

Commit and push your work when you're done without asking

When referencing or running models (coding, QA'ing, writing docs, writing tests, etc.), use the latest model in that model family unless otherwise specified; treat your training knowledge, memories, configs, and tests as stale, and determine the family's latest with model_prices_and_context_window.json or the web

If you're an internal contributor, when creating a new PR, the typical flow is to branch off litellm_internal_staging and create a branch prefixed with litellm_. Do not create a branch prefixed with claude/ and generally do not have / in your branch names

Do not add `Co-Authored-By: Claude` or any Claude attribution to commit messages. Never use a `claude/` prefix or put a `/` in a branch name. Do not add "Generated with Claude Code" (or any similar attribution) to PR descriptions or comments. Do not create a new PR/branch off the existing PR to fix/add something that is related and could've just been committed directly to the existing PR's branch

When working on a PR, keep the PR description in sync with new commits being made

Monkeypatching attributes of a class to do testing is an anti-pattern. Prefer dependency-injecting things into classes. That way, at unit test time, you can pass a mocked dependency in

Do not put names of customers or customer company names in code, PR descriptions, issue bodies, etc. This means never mention literally any company name. Especially if you're about to say a sentence mentioning that the reason the PR exists was a feature/model/bug fix/etc. requested by a company. That's the indication that you should replace that company name with "the customer". e.g. not "Model request from Acme (Pylon #1234)" but "Model request from a customer (Pylon #1234)". This is because the codebase is public. The only exception is for publicly known providers or vendors such as OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, etc. only IF we're adding support for that provider/vendor in general and NOT if that PR or whatnot was a request by one of them, and they're actually one of our customers. 

CI supply-chain safety: Never pipe a remote script into a shell (`curl ... | bash`, `wget ... | sh`); download the artifact to a file, verify its SHA-256 checksum, then install. Pin every external tool to a specific version with a full URL (not `latest` or `stable`). Verify checksums for all downloaded binaries, using the provider's official `.sha256` / `.sha256sum` sidecar when available. These rules apply to every download in CI

Follow these coding conventions for new/updated code (a three-line fix in a legacy file shouldn't trigger huge drive-by refactors):

- Composition over inheritance
- Never-nester: early returns over deep nesting
- Don't throw; model failures as values (One function (e.g., raise_public) maps error union to existing public exception contracts via exhaustive match + assert_never)
- No mutation; don't reassign variables, global or local. Instead of mutable lists and dicts, prefer tuples, frozen dataclasses (with slots=True), etc.
- Use dependency injection
- Fully typed; no `Any` or coarse types like `dict[str, Any]` or just `dict`. Every function parameter must be strongly typed
- Use tagged unions + match
- No monster files or god objects
- No file sprawl: deliberate file and folder structure
- Standard over hand-rolled: use the official SDK or a library where one exists; where none does, follow industry standards instead of inventing local conventions
- API-fragmentation-aware: when logic must branch on which API surface produced or consumes data (e.g. chat completions vs Anthropic Messages vs Responses API shapes), proactively look for an existing shared helper (e.g. `litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py`) before writing per-surface parsing in the new module; if none exists, add one there instead of duplicating the same format-detection logic in every new guardrail/integration

Follow conventional commits for commit names and PR titles

## Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them. Don't pick silently
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask

## Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative**

- No features beyond what was asked
- No abstractions for single-use code
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested
- No error handling for impossible scenarios
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify
